AI models are inevitably going to keep getting better and better at all coding, tool and computer use, math, and other coding-related tasks. As a result, agents that can use software to do their work, or generate code from scratch, will improve at a faster rate than all other domains of knowledge work.

On one hand that could mean that only a small subset of work can get automated. But probably what happens is that more and more work just becomes coding-shaped to adapt to what agents are good at.

You can see it in the most recent examples of model releases in the past couple of months, where agents can generate code that becomes animated videos, games, 3D models for products, and so on. We also know that tool use gives agents the ability to work with much of the same software that people already work with. This helps in cyber, life sciences, finance, and a number of other domains.

Our mental model traditionally has been that the models have to be able to know everything about anything to generate value, but in reality they *really* have to know how to use or generate software effectively combined with deep domain expertise to make the right judgment calls inside of workflows. 

When you have that powerful combination, almost everything else gets unlocked. This is why the acceleration of agents in knowledge work is only going to increase from here.

Announcing Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index v2.1, upgrading FrontierCode and Terminal-Bench. Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 share the lead at 58

The Coding Agent Index measures models in agent harnesses; v2.1 of the Index upgrades FrontierCode from 1.1 to 2.0 and Terminal-Bench from 4.0 to 4.1.

Upgraded:

➤ FrontierCode-AA 2.0 (replacing FrontierCode v1.1): our implementation of Cognition's FrontierCode 2.0, comprising 132 real-world coding tasks graded on whether a repository maintainer would merge the agent's change

➤ Terminal-Bench 4.1 (replacing Terminal-Bench 4.0): the same 66 tasks, scored with updated verifiers that improve reliability and resistance to reward hacking

Staying in the Index: SWE-Atlas-QnA-AA

Key results:

➤ Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5 share the lead at 58: Claude Fable 5.2 scores 58 at both xhigh and high in Claude Code. Claude Opus 5.5 (max) scores 58 in Claude Code and, paired with GPT-6 Luna High, in Cognition's multi-model harness Devin Fusion CLI. Claude Fable 5.2 (max) scores 56 as more of its attempts hit task time limits. Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max, 56) in Claude Code and Gemini 4 Carbon (high, 55) in Antigravity CLI follow

➤ Index scores are lower in v2.1, driven by the upgrade to FrontierCode-AA 2.0: models score lower by 5 points on average. Codex with GPT-6.1 Terra (max) is the only configuration which didn’t fall between versions, sitting within 1 point of its prior score

➤ Cost per task varies ~30x among configurations scoring 48+: from $1.51 for Codex with GPT-6.1 Sol (max, 52) to $44.22 for Claude Code with Claude Fable 5.2 (max, 56)

Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3 from Perplexity score 70 and 64, respectively, on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1

@perplexity_ai has released Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3, updating their v1.2 flagship decision models. Compared to v1.2, Decider v1.3 maintains its #6 position while Decider Flash v1.3 moves up into the #10 position.

Key results:

➤ Decider v1.3 has strong decision-making and extraction capabilities. Decider v1.3 is the #4 model on AA-Paperclip with a score of 69. It improves 2 points over Decider v1.2. It is also the #3 model on EvalSafe-O*NET-AA with a score of 89, a 1-point improvement over Decider v1.2

➤ Decider Flash v1.3 is more capable than its v1.2 predecessor. Decider Flash v1.3 achieves a score of 64 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1, a 4-point improvement over v1.2 driven by a 12-point improvement on both AA-Symmetry and When2Call

➤ Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3 sit on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier. With a Cost per 1M Tasks of $68 for Decider v1.3 and $34 for Decider Flash v1.3, both models occupy positions on the Capability vs. Cost Pareto frontier

Additional model details:

➤ Context window: 256K tokens

➤ Pricing: $0.02 and $0.01 per 1M input tokens for Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3, respectively

➤ Multimodality: Text and image input

➤ Size: 27B and 4B for Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3, respectively

➤ License: Apache License 2.0

➤ Providers: Available through Perplexity’s first-party API

Subquadratic’s SubQ Snap 1.2 gains 5 points over SubQ Snap 1.1 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1, and is tied with Drex Max v1.1 and GLiDE v1.2 as the leading decision model

SubQ Snap 1.2 is the latest decision model from @subquadratic. Pricing is unchanged at $0.04 per 1M input tokens, and it supports a 384K token context window.

Decision Index v2.1 updates AA-Symmetry to v1.1. AA-Symmetry measures whether a model keeps the same decision and confidence when a question changes in ways that should not matter. v1.1 moves the answer options into the state and rewords them with the same meaning.

Key takeaways:

➤ SubQ Snap 1.2 scores 73 on the Artificial Analysis Decision Index v2.1, up from 68 for SubQ Snap 1.1: Drex Max v1.1 (73) and GLiDE v1.2 (73) are within 0.1 points. The largest gains are on AA-Paperclip (+8 points) and AA-Symmetry (+8 points).

➤ The AA-Paperclip gain comes from more documents answered fully correctly: the all-pass rate rises from 46% to 62%, level with Drex Max v1.1 (63%) and GLiDE v1.2 (62%).

➤ The gains on AA-Omniscience-Decision and HLE-MultiChoice come from abstention, not accuracy: non-hallucination rates rise from 85% to 89% and from 46% to 55%. Accuracy is flat at 21% and 9%. On AA-Omniscience-Decision, SubQ Snap 1.2 attempts 29% of questions, down from 33%.

this is a very important essay if you want to understand AI progress and how to measure it. i've been working on this for a few months now and i agree with almost everything here. here is a few additional (unstructured) thought:

--

1) slowdown factor: second order interactions in training LLMs

about ai progress that we see in math coming from ai research, i made a post about this exactly ~1 month ago and i totally agree, but one point i would add to dwarkesh's comment is that one thing that can slow down ai research progress is the number of "second order interactions"

i can't comment on what big labs know here, but at least in the open, it's really not clear how the full model training pipeline interacts together, and so even at each layer.

let's take pre-training and a change like making the KV cache smaller. it would allow us to hillclimb inference efficiency. many experiment as shown that this can be neutral (or even lead to gain) on validation loss, tho does it mean we get a better model for long context agentic tasks? lots of conflicting results here, minimax went from linear attention (M1) to full attention (M2) to sparse attention (M3), at the same time Kimi went from full attention (K1.5/K2) -> linear attention (K3). mistral large 4 found KV sharing hurts terminal bench 2 but not cross entropy, while dsv4.1 flash is one of the best small models and have an insane KV sharing pattern (only 1 layer computes KV on the decoder). most of the western oss model use SWA, most of the chinese oss one don't. this is only one example on a singular decision that have impact on everything else. in pre-training you can have different shape, arch, data, learning algorithm, tpp, scale, ect.. interacting together. and each of this element can also interact with mid and post training 

these are just a lot of possible interactions, i'd say much more than math, and as an automated researcher tries more changes the number of interactions will grow. compute remains the main bottleneck here, and there is a huge difference between closed american labs and the rest of the world.

important point is that there are ways to reduce compute needs in the "long term"* by finding better proxies, or spending more inference at the problem, i'm saying long term as it can be more intensive to find proxies at first since you need to validate them at scale and for that you need compute as well.

*long term here is not super long btw lol, some very random guess of mine would be that it can be months for oai/anthropic scale of compute, but maybe years for chinese labs for instance. there is also the question of how much the gap here change if frontier lab continue release their best model or not, i.e anthropic nerfing ai capabilities with mythos 5.2

--

2) data vs algorithm progress and how efficiency gain can be "misleading"

in general for training LLMs there are two types of improvements that you can make, either data or algorithmic

this is a big topic but imo the main difference is that data improvements feels much bigger partly because they are directly optimizing what we are measuring. i think everyone is familiar with benchmaxing but i'll take another example in pre-training

let's say you are measuring the CE on a mixture of held out documents (good example is the MAI paper here). the pre-training mixture that you are choosing will very naturally converge with the mixture of domains in the held out documents, and same for each domain (the different languages in code will be relatively similar to the ones you are evaluating against). if you are measuring between a random mixture with for instance less code because you care less about code (like older model from a few years ago), and one optimized for code, you will get INSANE efficiency gain. this is exactly what is happening in the magic blog that dwarkesh is citing. there is also the question of what held out document you have, i'm seeing a lot of new labs evaluating against their own held out codebase which are probably ai generated and hence would bias towards more synthetic data in pre-training for instance regardless of quality 

doesn't mean this is a bad way to do it, i'm just saying that this can be a bit misleading and that data and algorithm should be studied separately and we can't really compare those numbers imo

about algorithm, there are many more ways than looking at CE loss vs flops only btw. let's look at a niche example, say you are training on a giga large datacenter, you want a giga large batch size, so you need an architecture that is sample efficient at large batch size => you can go for matrix-based optimizers (can look at Muon/Adam T recently released that addresses this problem). this makes your efficiency gain being a plot with y axis loss, x axis batch size (it's more of a 3D plot btw as you still sweep flops/time for almost everything). you can also change the y axis and replace CE loss by smth else

-- 

3) about how we report and measure ai progress

about "ai having research taste" there is no benchmark for that, i've tried to do some effort here with my nanogpt experiment (have some newer results with newer model being more capable, just have to find the time to write a blog)

one interesting finding was how good anthropic models were compared to oai ones, and one of their biggest differentiating factors was navigating through the noise inherent to this bench and small scale ML experiment. i've also tried to test RL environments that teach "taste for things that scale", this was a side project and i didn't manage to make it work perfectly because it's a bit tricky to find the right scale and also quite compute intensive. but i'm 100% sure this is the way to go and something that anthropic/oai are currently training on, i'm really expecting this to work. also keep in mind that big labs have an insane database of experiments which happens to be extremely useful for creating such environments

one last thing here is that i think most labs right now are hesitating between reporting results to quantify progress and which intellectual property to release or not. @Sam_McCandlish made a post about that for the METR report and said that releasing metrics to quantify ai progress would accelerate other ai labs. while i disagree with this (you can see my answer there) i think this is a very important debate that should be discussed much more with different parties!

--

When having debates about “Should we pause AI?” I think it’s helpful to first establish a baseline by asking “Do you wish the laws of physics were such that building more advanced AI, from this point forward, would be harder for everyone than it looks like it will be?”

The pause question, for good reason, centers debate on strategy questions like "What would China do?", "Would the pause be 'used well'?", and "Would pausing here be politically tenable?" Asking the baseline question first lets you check agreement on a common premise for the pause debate: We're on a fragile trajectory and the possibility of strong RSI would be an unfortunate fact about the nature of reality, to the extent it puts humanity in a collective action problem.

Getting to ground on the baseline question is sort of a prerequisite for discussing the pause one, since it decides whether you're both fundamentally in a "solutions mindset" about the prospect of strong AI self-improvement and misalignment, or whether the real crux is upstream, like whether these things are plausible enough to be worth worrying about.

In some ways the new Fable is a monster. This is SimpleQA Verified from Epoch. There are few benchmarks like this where Fable 5.2 jaggedly jumped ahead of the entire pack.

For me there are two big indicators arriving next week that will tell us a lot about the shape of things going into 2027. I'm assuming two things happen next week: Anthropic releases their internal progress report (from which we will get updated numbers on RSI), and OpenAI releases GPT-6.2 Astra.

With the new Astra, we will see how OpenAI answers Fable, and Fable needs to be answered. They need to close the gap, but they also need to close the gap that doesn’t show up on benchmarks: that a lot of people love working with the new Anthropic models, particularly Opus 5.5. And this is starting to tip the table a little.  Also expect another huge math release simultaneously with the new Astra. The previous one took five weeks and produced 700 papers; they've had another five weeks since then. They have also been working on other Millennium problems. Don't be shocked by anything. 

Astra's capability, and if it catches or surpasses Fable, is the first one. The second is where Anthropic is on AL4. The AI Futures Project (the AI 2027 guys) predict that AL4 reached 50% last month. If that's true, that means it will probably hit 80% by January. And at that point, assuming the overall pattern holds, some of the work at Anthropic will be at AL5 - aka fully autonomous with no human input. Probably about 5–10% of work at Anthropic would be at that level. If this number is actually higher than 50%, then things are moving even faster than believed, and that would be a big update for a lot of people, including me, who already has pretty short timelines. Above AL4 50% in October would probably mean RSI before the end of the year. Or possibly, already. So, a very important week for finding out where we are, and where we are headed.
